pillar_reactions.evidence: Only referenced in passing as a value argument — 'the system that's already built around your body, your injuries, and especially your schedule' — never presented as a pillar on this call.

The prospect rejected the accountability layer as something he neither needs nor wants to pay for: 'the day-to-day or weekly and check-ins, like I don't think are something I'm needing or necessarily wanting. And I get that's what you guys normally do, obviously, and that's why you charge what you charge.' The rep conceded the point rather than defending it — 'you don't need some checking in on you every single day' — which removed the main justification for the price before the price was named.

anchors.raw: I'd rather just go get my trainer in person and pay him for, you know, two or three sessions a week for the same amount of money while I'm still here, type of thing
anchors.note: The comparison is not to a cheaper product but to an equally priced, higher-touch, in-person one. At $1,500/month the offer is competing directly against 8-12 in-person sessions, which is a losing frame and the reason the concession followed immediately.

anchors.raw: to pay more than $1,000 for a one-month program without all the additions seems a bit high
anchors.note: He priced the deliverable he actually wants — programming only — at $1,000 and never moved. The rep had already conceded that the additions are not needed, so the prospect's valuation was internally consistent and hard to argue with.

unmet_demand.want: A one-off tailored kettlebell programme built around his injuries and travel schedule, with a check-in every two weeks or once a month, at around $1,000
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is 1:1 coaching at 6 or 12 months whose price is justified by the accountability layer he explicitly does not want. There is no tailored programming-only tier; Primal University at $200/month is self-serve and not built around his body, so it does not meet the ask either.
